before.label: Political economy & economic theory
before.date_label: Classical and later nineteenth-century roots; subsequent historical adaptations
before.description: A contested body of explanation about production, distribution and exchange. Smith’s division of labour, Ricardo’s distribution problem, Mill’s institutional distinctions, Marshall’s treatment of markets and time, and Menger’s account of theory offer different resources. Historians adapt and criticize these arguments rather than inheriting one uniform model.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Adam Smith is an eighteenth-century precursor; Ricardo, Mill, and Marshall represent different nineteenth-century developments. This is not a single unchanging paradigm. Read Smith (1776), Ricardo (1817/1821), Mill (1848), Marshall (1890/1920), and Menger’s methodological intervention (1883) as differing arguments, not a linear succession.

after.label: Economic history
after.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000).

after.label: Consumption & material culture
after.description: Examines commercial promotion, household demand, goods’ changing value, taste, gender and provisioning. McKendrick, Brewer and Plumb distinguish commercial and social changes; de Vries connects consumption with household labor; Mintz links diets to colonial production. Anthropological and feminist approaches ask how objects acquire meanings and how consumer roles depend on unequal social relations.

after.scope_note: Demand, taste, provisioning, commodities, and material objects are not one theory; gender and empire connect consumption to production. Commodity circulation, cultural biography and goods as communication are distinct questions. De Vries acknowledges conflicting household interests; feminist research does not reduce women to consumers. Much of this selection concerns Europe and the United States; Mintz’s colonial production connects regions but does not make the coverage global in every respect.

verification.note: University-hosted primary transcription downloaded; chapter opening and pp. 43–48 consulted for Polanyi’s criticism of Smith’s barter account, his use of social anthropology and the distinction between market regulation, reciprocity and redistribution. added.citation: Jan de Vries, “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution,” Journal of Economic History 54(2) (June 1994): 249–270.

verification.note: University-hosted primary scan downloaded and visually read at pp. 249–252 and 259–264. Supports household labor/resource reallocation, demand, explicit use of historical demography, and qualifications about intrahousehold interests and ideal types. The article criticizes McKendrick’s gendered wording and discusses Sabean’s household critique. No claim that all households followed this trajectory; quantitative estimates and later reception not independently replicated.

economic.people: Reviewed the eleven inherited selections and their explanatory roles; added Polanyi, Gerschenkron, de Vries and the existing shared Pomeranz identity. Preserved women’s work, British social-economic history, French serial inquiry, Marxist development and quantitative/institutional differences. Wider histories of business, innovation and non-European industrialization remain explicit follow-up.
economic.works_and_arguments: Replaced Labrousse’s vague work description with a checked 1933 title; made Fogel’s lecture precise and its limits explicit; clarified North and Tawney. Added four contextual readings with primary arguments. No empty selection existed in this entry at the start of this batch.
economic.internal_distinctions: Preserved all seven existing approach IDs and added market society, different industrialization paths, household labor/demand and regional/global divergence. North’s incentives are distinguished from Polanyi’s market society, and neither is equated with Gerschenkron’s account of banks and states.
economic.incoming_connections: Specified de Vries’s actual use of demographic literature in edge_204. Added Polanyi’s explicit turn to anthropology and de Vries’s demand-and-labor intervention. Reassessed existing historical-economics, Weber, Marx, women and quantitative resources against their recorded scope instead of inventing new directions.
economic.outgoing_connections: Specified Pomeranz’s contribution to global comparison and his environmental affinity. Preserved Dobb/Tawney, Annales, empire and unequal-development qualifications. Added Polanyi’s targeted critique of Smith; the Rostow/Gerschenkron/North link remains a comparison without claiming a directly checked Gerschenkron–Rostow debate.
economic.evidence_and_interpretation: Consulted primary Polanyi, Gerschenkron, de Vries and Pomeranz extracts; used BnF for Labrousse metadata. Recorded edition distinctions, contested causal claims and limits of inherited Fogel evidence. Polanyi is also added to the neighboring political-economy selection as a critic without counting another review.

consumption.people: Reviewed all six inherited selections with distinct roles; added de Vries, Kopytoff, Douglas, Isherwood, de Grazia, Furlough and the existing Bourdieu identity. Distinguished anthropologists, an economist and historians; added feminist editors with a specific intervention. Euro-American concentration and further women’s consumer research remain explicit limitations.
consumption.works_and_arguments: Replaced six inherited omnibus source lists with references relevant to each selection; supplied contextual arguments behind already nonempty works. Distinguished original editions from later reissues and online publication dates. No previously empty work selections were filled by this batch.
consumption.internal_distinctions: Added eight approaches: commercialization, household labor, commodity histories, circulation/value, object biography, social communication, taste/social position and gendered consumption. Preserved production/labor/empire connections and did not treat consumption as replacing production.
consumption.incoming_connections: Specified the feminist edited intervention and added anthropological contributions through Appadurai/Kopytoff, with Douglas/Isherwood as a further distinct resource. Retained Bourdieu’s existing contribution and upgraded only its bibliographic check; cultural and economic affinities remain comparisons. Salmon remains a comparison, not a demonstrated genealogy.
consumption.outgoing_connections: Added de Vries’s specific contribution to economic explanation and strengthened Mintz’s global commodity connection with checked publisher support. Read Appadurai’s use of Simmel but did not invent a separate graph entry or assign Simmel to an unsuitable parent just to create an edge.
consumption.evidence_and_interpretation: Read primary de Vries passages on household conflict, McKendrick’s gendered wording and nonuniversal ideal types, plus Appadurai/Kopytoff opening extracts. Publisher descriptions support bounded book arguments; catalogue contents do not certify individual chapters. Preserved source-history records when upgrading metadata.

economic: Assess a bounded business/innovation comparison through Chandler or Mokyr and a non-European industrialization case; distinguish institutional, technological and household explanations instead of expanding a generic growth canon.

Compare Fogel’s earlier counterfactual and slavery research with contemporary criticism in the quantitative-history batch; the currently checked 1993 lecture supports later demography/nutrition, not disputed slavery estimates.

In the global-history batch, compare Pomeranz’s regional units and resource argument with a specific scholarly challenge, retaining the 2000 book as mapped coverage and later criticism as retrospective evidence.
consumption: Read a bounded primary pair from Carole Shammas, Lorna Weatherill or Amanda Vickery alongside McKendrick and de Vries; examine household evidence, women’s purchasing, inequality and the dating of consumer expansion.
Assess consumption in one additional non-European or colonial setting through scholarship centered on local consumers, beyond Mintz’s linkage of colonial production and metropolitan diets.

In the practice/anthropology batches, read a primary Distinction passage and assess historians’ actual uses of Bourdieu, Douglas/Isherwood and object biography; current contents/publisher checks do not establish field-wide reception.
